newsitem.title: USA: Gene linked with nose and throat cancer- U.S. study.
newsitem.headline: Gene linked with nose and throat cancer- U.S. study.

text.p: Researchers said on Tuesday they had identified a gene that could explain why so many Chinese people get a nose and throat cancer usually linked to smoking.
A study published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute said one version of the gene, known as CYP2E1, more than doubled the risk of nasopharyngeal cancer.
The effect was strongest among those who had never smoked and who had no exposure to "second-hand" tobacco smoke.
The tumor is usually rare but its highest incidence is in southeast Asia, suggesting a possible genetic component.
Allan Hildesheim and colleagues at the U.S. National Cancer Institute, working in Taiwan, questioned nearly 700 people about their smoking, drinking and eating habits.
Half the group had nasopharyngeal cancer and half did not.
The main risk factor seemed to be having two copies of the "bad" version of the CYP2E1 gene.
Those who had never smoked and who had the "bad" variant had nines times the risk of disease compared to those who had other versions of the gene.
The gene codes for production of an enzyme involved in processing nitrosamines, chemicals found in smoke, processed fish, meat and other substances linked with cancer.
The researchers said they did not know why they found their unexpected results.
